/-!
# Erdős Problem 383

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/383](https://www.erdosproblems.com/383)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos383

/--
Is it true that for every $k$ there are infinitely many primes $p$ such that the largest prime
divisor of
$$
  \prod_{i = 0}^k (p ^ 2 + i)
$$
is $p$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_383 : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ k, {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧ Nat.maxPrimeFac (∏ i ∈ Finset.Icc 0 k, (p ^ 2 + i)) = p}.Infinite := by
  sorry

end Erdos383

sources_consulted: T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problem #383, https://www.erdosproblems.com/383, read through https://web.archive.org/web/20260101000000id_/https://www.erdosproblems.com/383 (capture dated 2025-12-12).
Mathlib sources: Data/Nat/Factors.lean, Data/Nat/Prime/Defs.lean, Data/Nat/PrimeFin.lean, Data/Finite/Defs.lean, and Order/Interval/Finset/Nat.lean.

Local review guidance: STATEMENTS.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, and AGENTS.md; provided calibration indexes, all eight not_misformalizations cases, and past_misformalizations/pr00562.md, pr01152.md, pr01670.md, pr01922.md.
review.notes: The sole declaration, Erdos383.erdos_383, faithfully states the source's question. The quantifiers, inclusive product over 0 ≤ i ≤ k, primality condition, and largest-prime-divisor equality all match. Scratch checks in /workspace/review/scratch.lean compile successfully: they prove the product is at least 4 for prime p, verify the explicit largest-prime-divisor characterization, prove the harmless k = 0 case, and evaluate small examples. Thus maxPrimeFac's exceptional values at 0 and 1 cannot affect the claim. The live source returned a Cloudflare challenge; archived copies supplied the statement and remarks, and the current independent Erdős-problem database still records the problem as open.
